section_1.title: The Hook: Measuring the Infinite
section_1.content: Introduce the difference between 'counting' and 'measuring.' Use a character, 'Pixel the Robot,' who is trying to predict exactly how long a battery will last. Explain that in continuous worlds (time, weight, height), the probability of an exact value (e.g., exactly 5.00000... hours) is zero, necessitating a new way to look at probability.
section_1.example: Pixel the Robot's battery lasts between 4 and 6 hours. What is the chance it lasts exactly 5.000... hours? It's impossible to hit that exact point, so we look at ranges instead.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Discrete vs. Continuous
section_2.content: Visualize the transition from a Bar Chart (Histogram) to a Smooth Curve. Show a histogram of heights where bars get thinner and thinner as we collect more precise data. This sets the stage for the 'Curve' being the limit of these bars.
section_2.example: Visualizing a staircase (Discrete) turning into a smooth slide (Continuous) as the steps become microscopic.

section_3.title: Defining the PDF: It's Not a Point, It's a Shape
section_3.content: Define the PDF $f(x)$. Crucially, explain that the y-axis represents 'Density,' not 'Probability.' Show a Bell Curve (Normal Distribution) and explain that higher parts of the curve mean data points are more 'crowded' or likely to occur in that neighborhood.
section_3.example: A 'Density Map' of a park: Areas where people crowd together (high density) vs. empty corners (low density).

section_4.title: The Golden Rule: Probability = Area
section_4.content: Introduce the concept that probability is found by calculating the area under the curve between two points (Integration). Use an animation where a shaded region between 'Time A' and 'Time B' represents the likelihood of an event occurring in that window.
section_4.example: Shading the area under a curve from 4.5 to 5.5 hours to find the probability that Pixel's battery lasts between those two times.

section_5.title: The Two Pillars of a Valid PDF
section_5.content: Present the two mathematical constraints visually: 1. The curve never goes below the x-axis ($f(x) \ge 0$) because you can't have negative likelihood. 2. The total area under the entire curve must equal exactly 1 (100% certainty that something happens).
section_5.example: An animation of a shape-shifting blob that can change height and width, but its total 'ink' or mass must always sum to 1 unit.

section_6.title: Application: The Uniform Distribution
section_6.content: Apply the concept to a simple 'Uniform Distribution' (a flat rectangle). This makes the area calculation (Base × Height) intuitive before moving to complex calculus.
section_6.example: A bus arrives every 10 minutes. The PDF is a flat rectangle from 0 to 10 minutes with a height of 0.1. The probability of waiting 0-5 minutes is the area: 5 (base) × 0.1 (height) = 0.5 or 50%.

outline.title: Application: The Uniform Distribution
outline.content: Apply the concept to a simple 'Uniform Distribution' (a flat rectangle). This makes the area calculation (Base × Height) intuitive before moving to complex calculus.
outline.example: A bus arrives every 10 minutes. The PDF is a flat rectangle from 0 to 10 minutes with a height of 0.1. The probability of waiting 0-5 minutes is the area: 5 (base) × 0.1 (height) = 0.5 or 50%.

outline.title: The Two Pillars of a Valid PDF
outline.content: Present the two mathematical constraints visually: 1. The curve never goes below the x-axis ($f(x) \ge 0$) because you can't have negative likelihood. 2. The total area under the entire curve must equal exactly 1 (100% certainty that something happens).
outline.example: An animation of a shape-shifting blob that can change height and width, but its total 'ink' or mass must always sum to 1 unit.

storyboard.title: Application: The Uniform Distribution
lecture_lines: Imagine a bus arriving anytime within ten minutes.
This creates a flat, rectangular probability shape.
Calculate simple areas to find the wait time.
animations: Draw a flat rectangle from 0 to 10 with height 0.1 in light yellow (#FAFAD2).
Shade from 0 to 5; label base '5' and height '0.1' with arrows (#FAFAD2).
Display calculation '5 * 0.1 = 0.5' and highlight result in bright blue (#00BFFF).

storyboard.title: The Two Pillars of a Valid PDF
lecture_lines: First, the curve never drops below zero.
Negative probability is physically impossible in our world.
Second, the total area must equal exactly one.
animations: Show a curve dipping below x-axis; highlight negative part in red (#FF0000) with 'X'.
Correct the curve so it stays above the axis; change color to green (#00FF00).
Shade the entire area under the curve in soft purple (#E6E6FA).
Display the total area equation ∫ f(x) dx = 1 in bold white (#FFFFFF).
Add a '100%' label over the purple area to signify total certainty.

outline.title: Defining the PDF: It's Not a Point, It's a Shape
outline.content: Define the PDF $f(x)$. Crucially, explain that the y-axis represents 'Density,' not 'Probability.' Show a Bell Curve (Normal Distribution) and explain that higher parts of the curve mean data points are more 'crowded' or likely to occur in that neighborhood.
outline.example: A 'Density Map' of a park: Areas where people crowd together (high density) vs. empty corners (low density).

outline.title: The Hook: Measuring the Infinite
outline.content: Introduce the difference between 'counting' and 'measuring.' Use a character, 'Pixel the Robot,' who is trying to predict exactly how long a battery will last. Explain that in continuous worlds (time, weight, height), the probability of an exact value (e.g., exactly 5.00000... hours) is zero, necessitating a new way to look at probability.
outline.example: Pixel the Robot's battery lasts between 4 and 6 hours. What is the chance it lasts exactly 5.000... hours? It's impossible to hit that exact point, so we look at ranges instead.

storyboard.title: Defining the PDF: It's Not a Point, It's a Shape
lecture_lines: This smooth shape is the Probability Density Function.
The vertical axis represents density, not direct probability.
High peaks show where data points crowd together.
Flat valleys represent less likely measurement outcomes.
Together, they form a map of likelihood.
animations: Display formula f(x) (#FFFFFF) next to a light blue bell curve (#ADD8E6).
Label axes 'Density' and 'Value' in light gray (#D3D3D3).
Populate the curve with dots: many under the peak (high density) and few in tails (low density).

storyboard.title: The Hook: Measuring the Infinite
lecture_lines: Meet Pixel, a robot measuring battery life precisely.
Counting discrete objects is simple and exact.
Measuring time involves infinite possible values.
The chance of hitting exactly five hours is zero.
Instead, we look at the probability of ranges.
animations: Show 5 colorful marbles (#FFD700, #ADFF2F, #00FFFF, #FF69B4, #FFA500) labeled 1-5.
Introduce Pixel the Robot (#C0C0C0) and a draining green battery (#32CD32).
Show timeline [4, 6] with a needle pointing exactly at 5.0. Zoom in on the point.
Needle at 5.0 shrinks and disappears; display P(X=5) = 0 in red (#FF0000).
Highlight interval [4.5, 5.5] on the timeline with a blue glow (#87CEFA).

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section6Scene(TeachingScene):

        title = "Application: The Uniform Distribution"
        lines = [
            "Imagine a bus arriving anytime within ten minutes.",
            "This creates a flat, rectangular probability shape.",
            "Calculate simple areas to find the wait time."
        ]
